column2: If verifiability is set to 1, does it mean that all information about providers are set?
column4: Short answer: No — verifiability = 1 means "all verifiability metrics that the system computes reached their maximum according to the scoring model," not automatically that every possible piece of provider information exists or has been independently validated.

column1: Explanation and caveats

- Verifiability is an aggregate (a weighted linear combination) of a set of individual metrics (e.g., presence of author/publisher metadata, license retrievable, VoID/DCAT metadata, signed data, presence of contact, examples, "is on a trusted provider list", etc.). If every one of those measured metrics scores maximum, the aggregated verifiability score becomes 1.

- Which provider fields are required to reach 1 depends on which individual metrics are included in your implementation and on their weights. A score of 1 only proves that the measured items are present (and satisfy whatever checks those metrics perform), not that:
- every conceivable provider field (every email, every contributor name, alternate contacts) exists, or
- the provider identity has been verified beyond the metadata (e.g., validated owner of an email or domain), or
- the metadata values are correct or up-to-date (only that the checks passed).

- Some checks may be binary (present/absent), some may be fuzzy, and some metadata items may be outside the verifiability metric set entirely. So one dataset could get verifiability = 1 while still lacking particular provider details that the system does not check.
How you can confirm provider information yourself
1. Inspect the metadata (VoID / DCAT or the dataset landing page) for explicit provider fields:
- dcterms:creator, dcterms:publisher, dcterms:contributor, dcterms:source, schema:creator / schema:publisher
- foaf:mbox, vcard:hasEmail, schema:contactPoint
- dcterms:identifier (DOI), landing page URL
2. Check whether the dataset is listed on a trusted-provider list / registry (relevant metric if present).
3. Check for machine-readable license and for signatures if your workflow requires them.
4. If you have a SPARQL endpoint you can run queries to extract provider metadata. Example (conceptual):
SELECT ?p ?o WHERE {
?s a void:Dataset .
?s ?p ?o .
FILTER (?p IN (dcterms:creator,dcterms:publisher,dcterms:contributor,dcterms:source,foaf:mbox,schema:contactPoint))
(Adapt prefixes and IRIs to your environment.)
5. Verify contact data manually if identity/trust is critical (e.g., check email domain, website, known repository).
